buddhism.1: Newcomers are met with calm voices, meditation cushions, tea and the promise of peace.
buddhism.2: Buddhist centers may offer meditation, retreats, tea and a peaceful refuge.
buddhism.3: Buddhism can future-fake through enlightenment, nirvana, better rebirth and merit.
buddhism.4: A student leaving may be told they are running from suffering or clinging to ego.
buddhism.5: Institutional Buddhism can devalue by defining ordinary desire as the root of suffering.
buddhism.6: A student says a teacher was abusive and hears, "Notice your aversion."
buddhism.7: Students are told to test the teachings, but negative findings are diagnosed as ego.
buddhism.8: Breakthroughs credit the method and teacher; dry months indicate your hindrances.
buddhism.9: A seeker begins meditation, then must attend retreats and stop trusting anger.
buddhism.10: "Nonattachment" can mean freedom from craving, but also suppression or tolerance of abuse.
buddhism.11: A teacher may accuse a questioning student of ego, shielded by robes and titles.
buddhism.12: A student reports teacher abuse, and the sangha may deny it or cite skillful means.
buddhism.13: Practitioners can become desensitized to reading pain as attachment and anger as ego.
buddhism.14: Buddhism can isolate through sangha dependence, retreat culture and teacher authority.
buddhism.15: Buddhism can triangulate through teacher, sangha, lineage and senior students.
buddhism.16: A harmed student may hear from senior students: "You are attached to anger."
buddhism.17: A student reporting teacher abuse may be labeled angry, attached, egoic or unstable.
buddhism.18: A student reports teacher abuse and is told to sit with anger and examine projection.
buddhism.19: A student "chooses" teacher authority after being taught that resistance is ego.
buddhism.20: The teacher names craving and ego as the cause, then offers meditation as relief.
buddhism.22: Teachers may control through compassion language: "This is practice."
buddhism.23: Students may be treated as spiritually immature if they trust anger, grief or moral alarm.
buddhism.24: Buddhist practice can erode identity by turning desire, anger and selfhood into problems.
buddhism.26: Buddhist centers may rely on dana, retreat fees, book sales and unpaid service.
buddhism.27: Communities may manufacture crisis by framing departure as running from suffering.
buddhism.30: Anger is welcome as something to observe, but anger at the teacher becomes ego.

dawoodi-bohra.30: No source records responsibility placed on families rather than the institution.

indigenous.1: People may be drawn through ceremony, ancestry, elders and the promise of returning.
indigenous.2: Traditions may offer ceremony, healing, elder guidance and recovery of identity.
indigenous.3: Ancestral systems can future-fake through ancestral blessing and restored identity.
indigenous.4: Someone leaving may be pulled back through elders, family and claims of protection.
indigenous.5: Ancestral systems can devalue through lineage obligation, ancestral fear, elder authority.
indigenous.6: A person questions an elder or healer and is told they are disrespecting the ancestors.
indigenous.7: Questioning an elder's demands is said to prove colonization has claimed their mind.
indigenous.8: Landing readings build the practitioner's reputation; ambiguous ones blame the client.
indigenous.9: A reconnecting person must then accept elder authority, secrecy, offerings and initiation.
indigenous.10: "Respecting ancestors" can mean remembrance, obedience to elders, payments or silence.
indigenous.11: Elders may accuse dissenters of disrespecting ancestors to protect their own authority.
indigenous.12: A person reports abuse, and the response may say outsiders cannot understand sacred ways.
indigenous.13: Reconnecting people may be normalized into elder authority, ritual secrecy and offerings.
indigenous.14: Ancestral systems can isolate through elders, secrecy and claims of outsider ignorance.
indigenous.15: Ancestral traditions can triangulate through elders, ancestors, spirits, clan and healers.
indigenous.16: A person questioning an elder may be pressured by relatives, initiates and elders.
indigenous.17: A person who questions elders may be labeled colonized, disrespectful, or cursed.
indigenous.18: A person questions an elder or abuse and is told outsiders cannot understand.
indigenous.19: A reconnecting person "chooses" initiation after being told the ancestors are calling.
indigenous.20: A person told they are cursed or disconnected finds relief through ceremony and offerings.
indigenous.21: A person questions an elder and is told they are disrespectful, colonized or cursed.
indigenous.22: Elders may control through ancestry, spirits, secrecy, initiation and protection language.
indigenous.23: Elders may treat younger or reconnecting people as too ignorant to question.
indigenous.24: Identity may be rebuilt around ancestors, land, bloodline, spirits and elders.
indigenous.25: Abuse by elders may be bypassed as initiation, testing, cleansing or sacred secrecy.
indigenous.26: Financial control may appear through offerings, initiation fees and healer payments.
indigenous.27: Crisis may be manufactured through warnings of angry ancestors, curses and spirit attack.
indigenous.28: A person who questions elders or payments may be labeled disrespectful or colonized.
indigenous.29: A questioning reconnecting person may be replaced by another seeker hungry for belonging.
indigenous.30: Elders may call payment or obedience voluntary, while refusal means losing protection.

judaism.1: Converts or returnees may be embraced through Shabbat dinners, holiday meals and songs.
judaism.2: Jewish communities may offer meals after birth or death and burial societies.
judaism.3: Future faking can still appear through covenant destiny, messianic hope and continuity.
judaism.4: A Jew who distances may hear: "You're breaking the chain," "Don't let Hitler win."
judaism.5: Judaism can devalue through communal obligation, chosenness and ancestral suffering.
judaism.6: A Jew says communal pressure feels suffocating, and hears, "That is just responsibility."
judaism.7: Intermarriage or non-observance reclassifies the questioner from wrestling to lost.
judaism.8: Communal honor is dispensed in variable portions, tracking observance and donation.
judaism.9: A person participates culturally, then is expected to join synagogue and marry Jewish.
judaism.10: Judaism may be called religion, ethnicity, culture or covenant depending on the pressure.
judaism.11: Communities may accuse leavers of betraying continuity, making identity communal property.
judaism.12: A person names abuse and is asked, "Why are you airing Jewish problems publicly?"
judaism.13: Communal obligation becomes normalized through holidays, Hebrew school, marriage pressure.
judaism.14: Judaism can isolate through peoplehood, continuity, synagogue life and endogamy pressure.
judaism.15: Judaism can triangulate through parents, rabbis, Holocaust memory, ancestors and children.
judaism.16: A Jew who distances may be contacted by parents and rabbis: "You're breaking the chain."
judaism.17: Internal critics may be accused of giving ammunition to antisemites or being self-hating.
judaism.18: A person reports abuse or corruption and is told not to air Jewish problems publicly.
judaism.19: A person "chooses" continuity while told ancestors suffered and assimilation must not win.
judaism.20: Jewish communal life can bond through collective trauma, exile and Holocaust memory.
judaism.21: A person trying to leave is pulled back through ancestors, children and family grief.
judaism.22: Expectations around marriage, children and synagogue may be framed as care for survival.
judaism.23: Adults may be treated as irresponsible if they do not marry Jewish or raise Jewish kids.
judaism.24: Jewish identity may be religion, ethnicity, history or covenant, and absorb the person.
judaism.26: Jewish financial control may operate through synagogue dues, day school and donations.
judaism.27: Communities may manufacture crisis through assimilation panic and demographic anxiety.
judaism.28: A Jew who marries out or leaves synagogue life may be treated as breaking the chain.
judaism.29: A person who marries out is contrasted with peers who marry Jewish.
judaism.30: A community can say belief is not required, then pressure practice, marriage and children.

orthodox-hasidic-judaism.1: Baalei teshuva may be welcomed with Shabbos meals, housing support and a total world.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.2: Communities may provide housing help, schooling, food and matchmaking.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.3: Marry properly, have many children, keep Shabbos, and you secure your place in the chain.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.4: Someone who leaves may face immediate pressure from parents, rabbis and former friends.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.5: Communities can devalue the individual by making the community the source of identity.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.6: A young person questions restrictions and is told the outside world influenced them.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.7: A Hasidic teen is told their doubts prove the outside world has infected them.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.8: Moments of favor, like a rebbe's gaze, are distributed unpredictably across chasidim.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.9: Baalei teshuva are praised for becoming observant, then requirements intensify.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.10: Rules may be called protective customs, binding halacha or community norms.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.11: Systems may accuse leavers of being corrupted while using restricted education.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.12: A young person reports abuse; the response may be denial, then "off the derech."
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.13: Children are normalized from birth into total community: dress, food, language, school.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.14: Communities can isolate: separate schools, controlled media, arranged marriage networks.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.15: Communities triangulate through rabbis, parents, matchmakers, yeshivas and reputation.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.16: A less observant young person may be approached by parents, rabbis and teachers.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.17: Leavers may be labeled off the derech, corrupted, unstable, rebellious or mentally ill.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.18: Abuse may be handled through rabbis and internal systems rather than outside authorities.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.19: Children "choose" observance after limited secular education and few exit tools.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.20: Insular communities create intense bonds by making the community the entire world.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.21: A person raised inside may lack secular education, outside contacts and independence.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.22: Insular education, strict modesty and media restriction are framed as protection.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.23: Adults may remain under rabbinic, family and communal authority for marriage and dress.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.24: Identity is shaped from childhood through clothing, language, schooling and authority.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.25: Abuse may be bypassed through avoiding lashon hara or preserving family honor.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.26: Financial control can be structural: kosher food, large families, yeshiva tuition.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.27: Insular communities may manufacture crisis around internet access and secular education.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.28: Someone who goes off the derech may lose family warmth, school access and housing help.
orthodox-hasidic-judaism.30: Communities say members freely choose observance, but children have limited exposure.

scientology.1: The hook often begins with a free personality test or introductory course.
scientology.2: Scientology often begins with free or low-cost entry points like tests and courses.
scientology.3: Scientology future-fakes through "Clear," Operating Thetan levels and total freedom.
scientology.4: A person pulling away may receive calls, letters, visits and ethics handling.
scientology.5: Scientology devalues through its diagnosis of the reactive mind, engrams and out-ethics.
scientology.6: A person says auditing harmed them and hears, "You have missed withholds."
scientology.7: Observing critical media or ex-member accounts is a suppressive act.
scientology.8: The Bridge is a purchase-metered ladder; the next release is one invoice away.
scientology.9: A person begins with a personality test, then needs auditing, more courses and more money.
scientology.10: Scientology presents itself as religion, self-help or philosophy depending on context.
scientology.11: Scientology may accuse critics of being suppressive, criminal or insane.
scientology.12: A person reports harm from auditing, and Scientology denies abuse.
scientology.13: Scientology normalizes invasive auditing, confessional files, disconnection and payments.
scientology.14: Scientology isolates through disconnection, suppressive person labels and ethics handling.
scientology.15: Scientology triangulates through auditors, ethics officers, registrars and supervisors.
scientology.16: Scientology can use auditors, ethics officers, family and disconnection pressure.
scientology.17: Critics may be labeled suppressive persons, criminals, degraded beings, liars or insane.
scientology.18: A member raises concerns and is routed into ethics or auditing, not given an answer.
scientology.19: A person "chooses" courses after a personality test identifies their ruin.
scientology.20: Scientology identifies a person's "ruin," then offers auditing and courses as relief.
scientology.21: A member objects and is routed into ethics, auditing or word clearing.
scientology.22: Auditing, disconnection and expensive courses are framed as tools for spiritual freedom.
scientology.23: Members are told their reactive mind and engrams make them unreliable without the tech.
scientology.24: Scientology redefines the person through reactive mind, engrams, overts and levels.
scientology.25: Distress is bypassed as reactive mind, engrams, overts or suppressive influence.
scientology.26: Scientology may charge escalating fees for auditing, courses and Bridge progress.
scientology.27: Scientology may manufacture crisis by identifying a person's "ruin" and calling it urgent.
scientology.29: A member who leaves is labeled suppressive and replaced by newer recruits.
scientology.30: Scientology can present itself as religion, self-help or applied philosophy by context.

sikhism.1: Newcomers can be deeply moved by langar, where everyone sits together.
sikhism.2: Sikh communities offer langar, hospitality, seva, music and practical support.
sikhism.3: Sikhism offers union with God, liberation from ego, divine remembrance and belonging.
sikhism.4: A Sikh distancing may be told they are forgetting the Gurus or dishonoring the panth.
sikhism.5: Sikhism can devalue through community honor, visible identity and family obligation.
sikhism.6: A Sikh who questions visible identity may be told they are ashamed of who they are.
sikhism.7: Questioning gurdwara committees or jathedars is framed as attacking the Panth itself.
sikhism.8: Recognition for sewa is unpredictable, which quietly converts devotion into competition.
sikhism.9: A Sikh participates in gurdwara life, then must keep hair, marry appropriately, do seva.
sikhism.10: Visible identity may be called devotion, communal duty or family honor by pressure.
sikhism.11: A Sikh who cuts hair may be accused of shame or weakness.
sikhism.12: A person names gurdwara corruption, and the response may be denial: "That is not Sikhism."
sikhism.13: Visible identity, family honor and seva can become inseparable from being Sikh.
sikhism.14: Sikh isolation can occur through family honor, gurdwara community and visible identity.
sikhism.15: Sikh triangulation can run through parents, gurdwara, sangat, panth and Gurus.
sikhism.16: A Sikh who cuts hair may be pressured by parents, relatives and gurdwara elders.
sikhism.17: A Sikh who cuts hair may be smeared as ashamed, weak, assimilated or disrespectful.
sikhism.18: A person raises gurdwara corruption and is told not to create division in the sangat.
sikhism.19: A person "chooses" visible identity while family honor and martyr memory attach to it.
sikhism.20: The community may bond people through pride, sacrifice, martyr memory and family honor.
sikhism.21: A person who tries to change appearance faces family shame and community gossip.
sikhism.22: Family and community may control hair and marriage under the language of dignity.
sikhism.23: Adults may be treated as immature if they cut hair or question gurdwara politics.
sikhism.24: Identity may be shaped through hair, turban, kirtan, gurdwara and panthic belonging.
sikhism.25: Family or community harm may be bypassed through honor, sacrifice and seva.
sikhism.26: Sikh financial control may appear through gurdwara donations and wedding expenses.
sikhism.27: Sikh communities may manufacture crisis around hair, turban and intermarriage.
sikhism.28: A Sikh who cuts hair may be treated as ashamed, assimilated or dishonoring the panth.
sikhism.29: A person who cuts hair is compared with someone who preserves visible identity.
sikhism.30: Pressure around hair and turban may be described as pride and remembrance, not control.

tibetan-buddhism.1: A seeker may be captivated by colorful ritual, mantras, initiations and secret teachings.
tibetan-buddhism.2: Communities may offer blessings, empowerments, retreats and an ancient esoteric path.
tibetan-buddhism.3: Tibetan Buddhism offers an enormous future: enlightenment, reincarnation and merit.
tibetan-buddhism.4: A student leaving may be told they are breaking samaya or jeopardizing future lifetimes.
tibetan-buddhism.5: Tibetan Buddhism can devalue through guru devotion and tantric secrecy.
tibetan-buddhism.6: A student says a lama exploited them and hears, "You are misperceiving."
tibetan-buddhism.7: Students take samaya vows binding them to the guru, often before knowing what is asked.
tibetan-buddhism.8: Teachings arrive on the lama's timetable, and withholding raises their price in devotion.
tibetan-buddhism.9: Students move from meditation into vows, empowerments, guru devotion, secrecy and loyalty.
tibetan-buddhism.10: "Skillful means" can describe compassionate teaching or excuse cruelty and misconduct.
tibetan-buddhism.11: A lama may accuse critics of broken samaya, ego or impure perception.
tibetan-buddhism.12: A student reports abuse by a lama, and the response may call it tantric method.
tibetan-buddhism.13: Students are normalized into guru devotion, then fear of karmic damage if they question.
tibetan-buddhism.14: Tibetan Buddhism can isolate through guru devotion, samaya, secrecy and lineage loyalty.
tibetan-buddhism.15: Tibetan Buddhism triangulates through lama, lineage, samaya and senior students.
tibetan-buddhism.16: A student questioning a lama may be approached by senior disciples warning about samaya.
tibetan-buddhism.17: Critics of a lama may be smeared as samaya-breakers, impure, ego-driven or faithless.
tibetan-buddhism.18: A student questions a lama's misconduct and is told not to break samaya.
tibetan-buddhism.19: Students consent to vows and guru devotion before fully understanding samaya.
tibetan-buddhism.20: The lama is idealized as a rare karmic connection, then may frighten students with samaya.
tibetan-buddhism.21: A student cannot challenge the lama without being warned about samaya and karma.
tibetan-buddhism.22: Guru devotion is framed as the highest form of spiritual care.
tibetan-buddhism.23: The lama may be treated as spiritually superior, making adult students childlike.
tibetan-buddhism.24: Student identity can be absorbed into guru devotion, lineage, samaya and vows.
tibetan-buddhism.25: Abuse by a lama may be bypassed as wrathful compassion, purification or skillful means.
tibetan-buddhism.26: Students may pay for empowerments, retreats, teachings, ritual objects and offerings.
tibetan-buddhism.27: Groups may manufacture crisis through samaya fear and karmic consequences.
tibetan-buddhism.28: A student who questions the lama may be treated as a samaya-breaker or impure.
tibetan-buddhism.30: A lama's authority may be absolute in practice but deniable in theory.
